metadata.note: New York's original elevated railways -- the rapid transit that came before the subway and filled the 1868-1904 gap on this map. The Ninth Avenue El of 1868 was the first elevated railway in the world, a cable-hauled experiment up Greenwich Street; steam took over in 1871, the four Manhattan lines were consolidated under the Manhattan Railway Company in 1879, and the IRT leased and electrified them in 1903. All four were then killed by the subways built to replace them: Sixth Avenue in 1938, Ninth Avenue and most of Second Avenue in 1940, the rest of Second Avenue in 1942, Third Avenue in Manhattan in 1955, and the Bronx stub of the Third Avenue El in 1973. IMPORTANT: unlike cities/new_york_subway.geojson, which uses real MTA track geometry, these alignments are STREET-CENTERLINE APPROXIMATIONS -- the structures are gone, so each route is reconstructed by following the present-day centerlines of the streets the el is documented to have run above (median longitude per latitude bin from OpenStreetMap way geometry), not digitized from period maps. Brooklyn's elevated lines are not here: the ones that survive are in the subway file as the Jamaica, Myrtle Avenue, Culver, Brighton and Fulton Street corridors.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: Geometry is approximate and is the weakest part of this file. Alignments follow modern street centrelines, so they do not show where an el ran over a private right-of-way, cut a diagonal, or curved between streets -- most conspicuously the Ninth Avenue El's 110th Street 'Suicide Curve' onto Eighth Avenue, the downtown approaches from South Ferry over Pearl and Front Streets, and the Third Avenue El's Bronx route, where there is an unmapped gap of roughly a kilometre between the end of Third Avenue and the start of Webster Avenue that is drawn here as a straight line. Station locations are not modelled at all. Branches and spurs are omitted: the Second and Third Avenue City Hall spurs, the Queensboro Bridge spur of the Second Avenue El (opened July 23 1917), the 34th Street and Polo Grounds branches, and the connections between the Sixth and Ninth Avenue Els at 53rd Street. All headways are estimated -- no timetable research has been done -- and the single 22 km/h speed applied to every line and era ignores the difference between 1870s steam and post-1903 electric operation, and between local and express tracks. The Bronx Third Avenue El's 1901 start year is the beginning of a construction period that ran to 1920, not a single verified opening date.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

segments.note: Opened July 1868 as the West Side and Yonkers Patent Railway, an experimental single-track cable-powered elevated from Battery Place up Greenwich St to Cortlandt St -- the first elevated railway in the world. Regular service began February 14, 1870; the cable kept breaking down and the company ran out of money. Frequency estimated/unsourced
